title: AI Compliance
subtitle: External law, not internal policy -- and it moves under you

slides.title: Governance vs. compliance
bullets: Module 12 asked: have we decided how to build AI responsibly?
Module 14 asks: does that satisfy a specific external law?
Compliance is what a regulator, auditor, or plaintiff's lawyer checks
Same raw material either way: model cards, evals, audit logs
13-ai-security = technical controls; this module = the law that requires them
slides.notes: Set the division of labor before anything else -- students conflate governance and compliance constantly.

slides.title: The warning that matters more than any fact in this deck
slides.quote: This is the module most likely to be wrong by the time you read it.
bullets: 2026 alone: a full EU AI Act timeline rewrite via Digital Omnibus
Colorado's AI law passed, delayed, then rewritten twice
A federal executive order attempting to preempt state AI law
Every date here was verified on a specific day -- re-check before relying on it
slides.notes: Say this out loud every time you teach this module. It is not throat-clearing, it is the actual lesson.

slides.title: Not legal advice
bullets: Nothing here -- least of all the code -- substitutes for counsel
Goal: technical fluency that makes a lawyer conversation productive
You bring a precise system description and specific questions
Counsel gives jurisdiction-specific classification and risk sign-off
The two scripts in this module are labeled 'educational scaffolding' for a reason
slides.notes: Repeat this before running the risk classifier demo -- it is easy to over-trust a tool that gives clean-looking output.

slides.title: Two philosophies, one problem
bullets: EU: horizontal law, ex-ante risk tiers, conformity assessment before market entry
US: no single statute, sectoral regulators stretch existing law over AI
EU trades slower deployment for pre-market assurance
US trades patchier coverage for avoiding a federal bottleneck
Ship globally -> you need fluency in both, not a favorite
slides.notes: Neither approach is 'ahead' -- they optimize for different failure modes. Resist the urge to pick a side.

slides.title: EU AI Act -- the four risk tiers
slides.notes: Classification is about USE, not sophistication -- a frontier LLM and a spam filter can both be minimal-risk.

slides.title: Tier 1: unacceptable risk (Article 5)
bullets: Social scoring by public authorities across unrelated contexts
Subliminal/manipulative techniques that cause harm
Exploiting age/disability/socio-economic vulnerability
Untargeted facial-image scraping; emotion inference at work/school
In force since 2 Feb 2025 -- no compliance path, only 'don't build it'
slides.notes: Emphasize: there is no accuracy level or safeguard that makes a prohibited practice acceptable.

slides.title: Tier 2: high-risk obligations (the heavy lift)
rows: Annex IV -- enough for an authority to assess
A human can understand, monitor, override
Self- or third-party -> CE mark + EU registration
slides.notes: Point at Module 12 for human oversight design and Module 15 for the testing surface -- this table is the bridge slide for the whole track.

slides.title: The separate track: general-purpose AI (GPAI) models
bullets: Regulates the MODEL, not the application -- hits foundation-model labs
All providers: technical docs, downstream info, copyright policy, training-data summary
Systemic risk: presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute
Systemic-risk models: red-teaming, incident reporting, cybersecurity, energy reporting
Fine-tuning a frontier model into a resume-screener: you inherit BOTH tracks
slides.notes: Neither track discharges the other -- a common misconception is that using a 'compliant' base model clears your application obligations.

slides.title: The timeline -- verify before you plan around it
slides.notes: The one-sentence version: prohibitions and GPAI rules are live now; heavy high-risk obligations got pushed well past their original date. Confirm current status before any date-sensitive decision.

slides.title: The US: a fragmented, fast-moving patchwork
bullets: No federal AI-Act equivalent -- NIST AI RMF is voluntary, not law
EO 14365 (Dec 2025) directs DOJ to challenge state AI laws as preempted
That fight is LIVE, not settled -- state laws remain enforceable until a court says otherwise
FTC: no AI-specific rulemaking, enforces Section 5 against AI-washing and dark patterns
The durable pattern: existing sectoral law absorbs AI, not new AI statutes
slides.notes: Ask the class: 'which existing law is this AI system now subject to' -- that question ages better than any specific citation.

slides.title: Colorado, as a case study in how fast this moves
slides.quote: If you built a compliance program against the 2024 text, most of it no longer maps to current law.
bullets: SB 24-205 (2024): comprehensive risk-based framework, Feb 2026 effective date
Delayed to June 2026
Days before that deadline: rewritten by SB 189 into a narrow disclosure law
New effective date: 1 Jan 2027 -- duty-of-care and impact assessments dropped entirely
slides.notes: This is the single best teaching example for 'do not treat any snapshot as permanent' -- three changes in 18 months.

slides.title: Sector rules layer on top of AI-specific law
slides.notes: The pattern: AI rarely gets a brand-new law, it gets absorbed into a regulator that already existed. Ask which regulator already owns this domain.

slides.title: GDPR, applied specifically to AI
bullets: Lawful basis needed for training data, not just for using the model
Article 22: right not to be subject to SOLELY automated significant decisions
No 'right to explanation' in the text -- but keep a human meaningfully in the loop
Data minimization sits in tension with pretraining at scale -- unresolved, not solved
RAG retrieving a personal-data chunk is a GDPR processing event, full stop
slides.notes: The RAG point surprises people every time -- the LLM in the loop changes nothing about the legal analysis of the retrieved data.

slides.title: ISO 42001 vs. SOC 2 -- what each actually certifies
rows: You run a disciplined AI risk process
Any specific model is safe or accurate
Existing trust-service criteria, applied to an AI feature
slides.notes: Treat ISO 42001 as 'we have a real governance program' -- a strong claim, but a different claim than 'our resume-screener is EU-AI-Act-compliant'.

slides.title: One artifact, many audiences
bullets: Model card -> most of an Annex IV entry + ISO 42001 impact record
Eval report -> the accuracy/robustness evidence + SOC 2 performance evidence
Trace/audit log -> record-keeping + human-oversight evidence, two frameworks at once
Risk register entry -> risk-management evidence for the Act AND ISO 42001
A new document with no engineering artifact behind it is a smell, not a requirement
slides.notes: This is the operating idea behind compliance_documentation_mapper.py -- run it live here if presenting.

slides.title: IP and copyright: genuinely unsettled
bullets: Bartz v. Anthropic: fair use for LEGALLY acquired training books (June 2025)
Separate piracy claim settled for $1.5B, approved July 2026 -- largest ever
NYT v. OpenAI: still actively litigated, no verdict -- don't cite an outcome
Open-weights license != legal freedom to use -- read the actual text every time
One district court ruling is precedent, not settled national law
slides.notes: Warn explicitly against treating the Anthropic settlement as 'training on copyrighted work is legal' -- it resolved a narrower piracy claim.

slides.title: Building a compliance program: start with a gap assessment
bullets: Not: read every regulation cover to cover
Instead: inventory what you actually have, map what applies to each item
Columns: use case, jurisdiction, sector, AI-act tier, data posture, owner, status
Re-run quarterly -- both your use cases AND the applicable rules move
The 'internal tool everyone forgot was AI' is a more common finding than you'd think
slides.notes: This table shape is exactly what code/eu_ai_act_risk_classifier.py and the mapper tool are built to feed.

slides.title: Working with legal counsel effectively
bullets: Bring: a precise system description, not a marketing one
Bring: your gap assessment as 'confirm or correct this', not a blank page
Bring: specific falsifiable questions, not 'is this compliant?'
Expect back: jurisdiction-specific classification and risk-tolerance decisions
Failure mode: 'counsel hasn't objected' treated as sign-off nobody actually asked for
slides.notes: Precision on your side buys precision on theirs -- this is the single most actionable slide for a working engineer.

slides.title: Exit check
bullets: Given a real AI use case, produce a one-page gap assessment
Which jurisdictions/sectors apply, which tier and obligations follow
Which existing artifacts already cover which requirement
What's actually missing, and what you'd ask a lawyer to confirm
Run both scripts in code/ against your own use case before you call this done
slides.notes: Close by running eu_ai_act_risk_classifier.py --demo live if you haven't already -- seeing four different tiers come out of one tool is the best proof this isn't hand-waving.
